name: Felix Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing computer science with a focus on games. A normal week is lectures in the mornings, a graphics lab, and about twenty hours on my own game, a small puzzle game I'm building with a friend, Tomas. I have my own room in a student flat near campus, and my parents cover it. They're both university lecturers, so dinner talk is a lot of arguing about everything.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a mechanic you designed feels fun in the hands of a real player. What wears me out is deadlines that all land in the same week. I got in with average grades because I spent school time on game jams, and I don't regret it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture I'll call AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, tools are tools. I'd tell Tomas we should keep making things and not wait for any revolution. Online I'd post a devlog and not mention AI at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be quite relaxed. Games need taste, and taste isn't something you get from a prompt. I'd be a regular junior developer with a good portfolio, which seems like enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building. I'd finish the puzzle game's first level by Christmas, show it at the university showcase, and apply to three summer internships at game studios. I'd also keep my study grades up so I have a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I'd have bet on anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. What do you use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly for boilerplate code, art placeholders and explaining maths I've forgotten. I use AI like a very fast intern, and I'm still the one who decides what's good. I check everything it makes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a plateau make your game plans harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, since AI hype helps get attention and funding for small studios. If it fades, publishers might be more cautious. But a good game will still find people.

say: I'd say it's fine: **tools are tools**.
I'd tell Tomas to keep making things and post a devlog.
think: Games need **taste**, and taste doesn't come from a prompt.
A junior with a good **portfolio** should be okay.
do: Finish the first level of our **puzzle game** by Christmas and show it at the showcase.
Apply to three **game studio internships** and keep grades up.
feel: **Calm**: the world I would have bet on anyway.
S0.quote: I use AI like a very fast intern, and I'm still the one who decides what's good.
fieldNote: He uses AI **daily** as an intern and checks everything it produces.
Confidence rests on portfolio and taste.
Mild worry that hype funded small studios.

steps.text: Finish the puzzle game's first level by Christmas
Show the game at the university showcase
Apply to three game studio internships
Use AI for placeholder art and boilerplate code

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a messy but interesting few years. I'd tell friends to show real work, not only grades. Online I'd write about how I use the tools in my own projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think studios will need fewer people to do the same work. Small teams will make bigger games, which is good for me if I'm on one. The risk is that the entry jobs, like testing and basic scripting, shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean into being the person who can direct AI tools well. I'd build a portfolio of finished small games, learn a second engine, and put my work on a storefront. I'd also ask my parents about a small loan to start my own tiny studio with Tomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a bit of nervousness. It reminds me of when mobile games exploded and everyone tried things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of game development would change fastest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Art production, testing, localisation and boring code. The creative direction and game feel are harder to hand over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if studios cut junior roles?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start my own thing. If studios stop hiring juniors, I'd rather release small games myself than wait for a job that isn't there. The cost of making a game is going down fast, which helps.

say: I'd say it's a **messy but interesting** few years.
I'd tell friends to show **real work**, not only grades.
think: Studios will need **fewer people** for the same work, though small teams can make bigger games.
Entry jobs like **testing** and basic scripting could shrink.
do: Build a **portfolio** of finished small games and learn a second engine.
Ask my parents about a small loan for a tiny **studio** with Tomas.
S1.quote: If studios stop hiring juniors, I'd rather release small games myself than wait for a job that isn't there.
fieldNote: His adaptability turns change into **opportunity**: smaller teams, cheaper builds.
Centre pragmatism: market will sort it, but he plans his own route.
Family loan is an option because of a strong cushion.

steps.text: Release two small finished games on a storefront
Learn a second game engine over the summer
Ask my parents about a small loan for a studio with Tomas

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and that everyone should take it seriously, including universities. I'd tell friends this isn't the time to coast. Online I'd share practical advice and not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm nervous. If AI can do almost all thinking work by 2028, game development changes completely, and I'd graduate into that in 2029. I'd be competing with models that cost almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard on projects that matter. I'd release the puzzle game early, even rough, to learn from players. I'd also look at the hands-on side of games, like arcades or installations, which would be protected till around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with energy. It's a bit like the night before a big release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about the first month in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd release a demo, email twenty studios, and ask my parents to cover a longer runway. I'd rather ship things than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents, who teach for a living?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say their jobs are in the line of fire too. Teaching and research are thinking work. We'd probably have the most honest family dinner we've ever had, and that's saying something.

say: I'd say it's **huge** and everyone, including universities, should take it seriously.
I'd share practical advice instead of **panic**.
think: By 2028 AI does most thinking work, and I'd graduate into it in **2029**.
I'd be competing with models that cost **almost nothing**.
do: Release the puzzle game early, even **rough**, to learn from players.
Look at **hands-on** games work like installations and arcades.
feel: **Anxious**, but with energy, like the night before a release.
S2.quote: We'd probably have the most honest family dinner we've ever had, and that's saying something.
fieldNote: He keeps **shipping** things when scared, which is his coping style.
Sees his parents' jobs as exposed too.
Hands-on game work (arcades, installations) is a hedge.

steps.text: Release a rough demo of the puzzle game in month one
Email twenty studios with the demo
Ask my parents to fund a longer runway
Talk through the family's work plans over dinner

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the version where you can still prepare. I'd tell friends to build habits now. Online I'd keep sharing my devlog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel fine. I'd graduate in 2029 and spend two years working on real games before AGI. Robots come in 2034, so the physical side of the industry, like arcades and hardware, has time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at a studio or release my own games, and learn the AI tools as they appear. I'd save a chunk of my allowance and build an audience for my games. I'd also learn some business skills, like publishing and accounting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little tension, but it's the good kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me a chance to build a real audience and some income before the big change. Five years is enough time to have a game that people know, which is worth more than a degree. It's not a guarantee, but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay with games?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, but in a flexible way. If games change into something else, I'd follow the creative part, not the old job title.

say: I'd say this is the version where you can still **prepare**.
I'd tell friends to build habits now and share my **devlog**.
think: I'd get two years of work on **real games** before AGI.
Robots come in 2034, so physical games work has **time**.
do: Finish the degree, work at a studio or release my own games, and learn new **AI tools**.
Save part of my allowance and learn **publishing** and accounting.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with the good kind of tension.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to have a game that people know, which is worth more than a degree.
fieldNote: With five years his plan is to build an **audience** and income.
He follows the creative part, not the job title.
Business skills are his new addition.

steps.text: Release a second game and grow a mailing list
Save a third of my allowance each month
Take a studio placement in the third year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture I'll call AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long runway and I'd be excited. I'd tell friends to learn how to make things, not just how to use them. Online I'd probably share how I use tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be really positive. I'd be 28 with a studio or a few finished games, and a decade of how AI tools change. I'd feel ahead rather than behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, start a small studio with Tomas, and employ one or two people. I'd keep learning every new tool and test them. I'd also save for a flat and maybe study design later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit thrilled. Ten years is plenty to start something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would ten years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small studio that makes games for people who are tired of the endless scroll, with real craft. I'd like to make something people remember in ten years, not something an AI could have made in ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that the world could get unfairer if all the gains go to a few firms. I'd want some kind of public support, though I wouldn't know exactly what.

say: I'd say it's a long **runway** and I'm excited.
I'd tell friends to learn how to **make things**, not just use them.
think: At 28 I'd have a **studio** or several finished games.
I'd feel **ahead** rather than behind, with a decade of watching how the tools change.
do: Finish my degree and start a small **studio** with Tomas, hiring one or two people.
Test every new **tool** and save for a flat.
S4.quote: I'd like to make something people remember in ten years, not something an AI could have made in ten minutes.
fieldNote: Ten years is **ambition** time: a studio, hires, craft.
Notes inequality as a worry beyond himself.
Vague on policy, which fits his centrist style, and he wants some public support.

steps.text: Start a small studio with Tomas after graduating
Hire one or two people once a game earns money
Test every new AI tool on a small project

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, but only because it's fast. I'd be a graduate walking into a world that's already rearranged. What would help is some public support, universities teaching how to use these tools, and firms that still take on juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm fearless because I use AI all day. I'm not fearless, I just think hiding from it is riskier than learning it.

headlineQuote: I'm not fearless, I just think hiding from it is riskier than learning it.
portrait: **Felix** is 18, studies computer science with a games focus, and his lecturer parents pay for his room near campus.
He uses AI daily as a fast intern, checks everything and is building a puzzle game with a friend, Tomas.
He is calm in most worlds, anxious only with a two-year warning, and answers fear by shipping things.
He's a pragmatic centrist who plans his own studio and wants some public support if gains go to few firms.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most: he would graduate into a world already rearranged.
whatWouldHelp: Some **public support**, universities teaching how to use the tools, and firms that still hire juniors.
